primitives.name: Kickoff Ball Trajectory
primitives.verbatim_quote: Stopping after the tensity of the kick-off while an official puts the ball in play at the twentyyard line seems in my experience to produce a certain perceptible let-down which sometimes spells disaster.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'v': 'Initial kickoff velocity (m/s)', 't': 'Time to first contact (s)', 'd': 'Distance traveled (m)'}
primitives.assumptions: Ball behavior follows deterministic path under idealized conditions.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When t exceeds 0.5s, risk of interception increases exponentially.

layer2.mapping: Ball trajectory modeled as a Markov chain in GSE; GSI infers risk via conditional probability of interception given time-to-contact.
layer2.telemetry: First contact time and distance to nearest defender

primitives.name: Kickoff Tactical Decision
primitives.verbatim_quote: In 1916 a momentary failure to realize this simple fact cost Princeton a touchdown and a game to Yale, when a kick-off which any one of three Princeton backs could easily have handled was allowed to bound about until a Yale player caught andcarried it over the line.
primitives.assumptions: Tactical decisions are made within bounded rationality constraints.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When D > 0.3s, R drops below 0.5, leading to loss of possession.

layer2.mapping: GSE evaluates decision tree branches based on D and C; GSI computes posterior probability of error given historical data.
layer2.telemetry: Decision latency vs. successful handling rate

The primitives form a triadic system: emotional regulation governs initial player readiness, ball trajectory defines physical dynamics, and tactical decision encapsulates cognitive processing. These interact in a feedback loop where emotional regulation influences decision-making speed (D), which in turn affects trajectory control (v). The breakdown regime occurs when D exceeds 0.3s, causing a cascade of failures in both tactical and physical execution. The system exhibits non-linear sensitivity to delays, with small perturbations in E or D amplifying into significant outcomes. This aligns with stochastic control theory where discrete actions (handling, catching) are governed by continuous state variables (velocity, timing). The dual nature of the system lies in its deterministic physics (trajectory) and probabilistic cognition (decision). Failure modes emerge from misalignment between these layers—emotional dysregulation leads to delayed decisions, which then propagate into suboptimal handling of the ball.
